subject: Coercing Real to Int for Poisson with Censored Data?

messages.author: d1237c2d244e29ff
messages.subject: Coercing Real to Int for Poisson with Censored Data?
parts:
I am working on analyzing data on the number of offspring reared to reproductive age as a function of the number conceived by a given woman, in order to investigate quantity quality tradeoffs in a non-industrial population.

There are three kinds of records:
1) Women who have complete conception records (women are either dead or >55 years old) and complete rearing records (all offspring are either dead or over 18).
2) Women who have complete conception records (women are either dead or >55 years old) and incomplete rearing records (some offspring are alive and under 18).
3) Women who have incomplete conception records (women are alive and under 55 years old) and incomplete rearing records.

The first kind of record is easily handled with a standard Poisson. The second kind of record can be handled by integrating over the censored records as described in the manual, since we know that the outcome is constrained to fall between the observed counts of reared offspring and the total count of conceptions minus offspring who have died.

The third kind of record is more challenging, since we need to impute the number of conceptions (given the location of the woman on the reproductive life course), this can be imputed as a real without much harm (i think) since it is inside the linear model for lambda. 

Next what I would like to do is for every imputed value of number of conceptions,X, take floor(X), and use this as the upper limit on the number of possible reared offspring when integrating out the censored records. This will limited the area of the CDF being integrated over to remain under the imputed number of conceptions.

To do this I need floor(X) to be an int, but it can't figure out how to make it so. I also don't know if this is 'shenanigans' given how HMC works.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Coercing Real to Int for Poisson with Censored Data?
parts:
On 10/11/13 4:02 PM, Cody Ross wrote:
>
> I am working on analyzing data on the number of offspring reared to reproductive age as a function of the number
> conceived by a given woman, in order to investigate quantity quality tradeoffs in a non-industrial population.
>
> There are three kinds of records:
> 1) Women who have complete conception records (women are either dead or >55 years old) and complete rearing records (all
> offspring are either dead or over 18).
> 2) Women who have complete conception records (women are either dead or >55 years old) and incomplete rearing records
> (some offspring are alive and under 18).
> 3) Women who have incomplete conception records (women are alive and under 55 years old) and incomplete rearing records.
>
> The first kind of record is easily handled with a standard Poisson. The second kind of record can be handled by
> integrating over the censored records as described in the manual, since we know that the outcome is constrained to fall
> between the observed counts of reared offspring and the total count of conceptions minus offspring who have died.

You might be able to use a difference of CDFs here, too,
depending on how simple the model is. The problem is when
the span gets big, you get a big summation in the direct
marginalization.

> The third kind of record is more challenging, since we need to impute the number of conceptions (given the location of
> the woman on the reproductive life course), this can be imputed as a real without much harm (i think) since it is inside
> the linear model for lambda.
>
> Next what I would like to do is for every imputed value of number of conceptions,X, take floor(X), and use this as the
> upper limit on the number of possible reared offspring when integrating out the censored records. This will limited the
> area of the CDF being integrated over to remain under the imputed number of conceptions.
>
> To do this I need floor(X) to be an int, but it can't figure out how to make it so. I also don't know if this is
> 'shenanigans' given how HMC works.

We've tried to discourage real to int conversions, as they lose the
gradient information in HMC. floor() is also bad if the value being
floored is a real parameter that needs to be estimated, because the
derivative is 0 everywhere but where the function's discontinuous.
Stan's search then becomes a random walk.

It might work anyway, but you'd need a way to get an int in order to
pass it into Poisson, which requires an int argument.

You could hack it up using int_step and a loop, but that's super ugly.

convert x to floor(x) as int

real x;
int floor_x;
{
floor_x <- 0;
while (!int_step(x - floor_x))
n <- n + 1;
v <- n;
}

But it's probably not a good idea.

Maybe you can code up the density you want using a real-value
in the CDF. You can use our floor() function for that because
it's fed into a gamma function. The Poisson's CDF is pretty simple:

http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poisson_distribution

Maybe somebody else will have a better idea.

Or maybe somebody will motivate the function:

int round(real);

But we'd have to red flag it everywhere because it's unsafe
in Stan. (We should probably also issue warnings on uses of
floor() for the same reason.)

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: Coercing Real to Int for Poisson with Censored Data?
parts:
Bob,

I like the suggestion for coding up a Poisson CDF as you have suggested.

Is it necessary to code up the CDF using the incomplete Gamma function? (Stan doesn't have an implementation of that yet correct?).

Or could I think up the problem as summing the Poisson PDF from i=0{or some value} to i=floor(X)? It would be nice to have floor(X), be available to use in a for loop, in this case.

Ignoring that the for loops will not all share "N," would something like this work? Floor X will stay small (<15, since these are births in a human life span)

 
######################################################################### Regressions
# Censored Class 1 - Uncensored  
  for (n in 1:N) {
Y[n] ~ poisson(exp(Lambda[n]));
  }
 
# Censored Class 2 - Uncensored Conceptions - Censored Recruitment
# Calculate the difference in CDFs between Y1=min.recruited possible, and Y2=max.recruited.possible  
  for (n in 1:N) {
  lp__ <- lp__ + log1m(poisson_cdf(MinY[n],Lambda[n])- poisson_cdf(MaxY[n],Lambda[n]));
  }

# Censored Class 3 - Censored Conceptions - Censored Recruitment
# Calculate the difference in CDFs between Y1=min.recruited possible, and Y2=max.recruited.possible , where Y2=floor(X), and X=number of conceptions
  for (n in 1:N) {
  cumulative_prob <- 0
  for(i in MinY[n]:floor(X)){
  cumulative_prob <- cumulative_prob + poisson_pdf(i,exp(Lambda[n]));
  }
  lp__ <- lp__ +  cumulative_prob
}

> Is it necessary to code up the CDF using the incomplete Gamma function? (Stan doesn't have an implementation of that yet

Oh, I didn't see that it used an incomplete Gamma. I would
guess that it is required if that's how it's written, but
I'm always surprised how things can be formulate differently.

> Or could I think up the problem as summing the Poisson PDF from i=0{or some value} to i=floor(X)? It would be nice to
> have floor(X), be available to use in a for loop, in this case.

You could do that, but you'd need to use a while loop.
For loops require integers in their bounds.

As before, it's going to break the tie to derivatives,
so sampling will probably be hampered by that (it shouldn't
be wrong, it just won't have gradients to guide it).

And it's "poisson_log" you want, not "poisson_pdf", though maybe
we should've called them _pmf and _pdf, or maybe just _pf.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: Coercing Real to Int for Poisson with Censored Data?
parts:
It appeared that Stan 2.0.1 may have provided a way I could easily code the smoothed interpolation of the Poisson CDF, using the incomplete upper Gamma distribution, as
Bob suggested. This should allow the model to run without reducing to a random walk.

The major likelihood statements of the newest version of the model are:
# Censored Class 1 - Uncensored

for (n in 1:N1) {
  increment_log_prob(poisson_log(Recruited[n],Lambda[n]));

}
 
# Censored Class 2 - Uncensored Conceptions - Censored Recruitment

# Calculate the difference in CDFs between min.recruited possible, and max.recruited.possible  
  for (n in 1+N1:N2+N1) {
  increment_log_prob(log_diff_exp(poisson_cdf_log(MaxRecruited[n],Lambda[n]), poisson_cdf_log(MinRecruited[n],Lambda[n])));    
  }

##Censored Class 3 - Censored Conceptions - Censored Recruitment
#Calculate the difference in CDFs between min number of recruited possible and number of imputed conceptions using inc gamma function for smoothly
#interpolated poisson_cdf
for (n in 1+N1+N2:N) {
 increment_log_prob(log(  (gamma_q((impConceptions[n]+1.01), Lambda[n])) - (gamma_q((MinRecruited[n]+1), Lambda[n]))    ));
        }

  I can't get the model to compile, however, as the code crashes both RStan and command line Stan. I cannot figure out why.

Some notes:

1) The code for censored class 1 and 2 runs fine (when code for class 3 is commented out). So it is the code for censored class 3 that crashes both RStan and command line Stan.

2) I can rewrite the code for censored class 2 using the gamma_q functions as in the code for censored class 3, and the model runs (when code for class 3 is commented out). So the issue doesn't appear to be with the coding of the interpolated Poisson CDFs.

3) impConceptions[n] is constrained to be >=MinRecruited[n], so the +1.01 inside the gamma function should ensure that first CDF is strictly greater than the second CDF. So Stan is never asked to evaluate the log of a negative number.

4) impConceptions[n] is a parameter estimated in the model, using a simple truncated regression of the form:
impConceptions[n] ~ normal(a + b*Exposure[n],SD)T[1,15];
where Exposure[n] is the time the woman has spent at reproductive age.

5) impConceptions[n] is also used in the definition of Lambda[n]
Lambda[n]<-exp( Theta1 + Theta2*log(impConceptions[n])) ;

Any advice would be much appreciated, if any additional info is required let me know what I should provide.

#########################################################  Stan Model
model_code<-"
data {
  int<lower=0> N;                           # Number of cases, total
  int<lower=0> N1;                          # Number of cases, censor class 1
  int<lower=0> N2;                          # Number of cases, censor class 2
  int<lower=0> N3;                          # Number of cases, censor class 3
  int<lower=0> NmissEx;                     # Number of missing "Exposure"
  int<lower=0> NmissC;                      # Number of missing "Conceptions"
 
  int<lower=0> Recruited[N];                # Number of children per woman actually recruited
  int<lower=0> Conceptions[N];              # Number of acutal conceptions/pregnancies per woman
 
  int<lower=0> MinRecruited[N];             # Only relavant to censored classes 2 and 3  (count observed at time of censoring)
  int<lower=0> MinConceptions[N];           # Only relavant to censored classes 2 and 3  (count observed at time of censoring)
 
  int<lower=0> MaxRecruited[N];             # Only relavant to censored classes 2 and 3 (=num conceptions in class 2, and =15 in class 3)
  int<lower=0> MaxConceptions[N];           # Only relavant to censored classes 3 (=15)
 
  int<lower=1> TimeID[N];                   # ID of time phase of subpopulation
  int<lower=1> LocID[N];                    # ID of location of subpopulation
 
 ############################################ Used to create transformed parameter vectors with varying lower and upper constraints
  int<lower=1> Nc[14];                      # Number cases of missings conceptions for each lower limit 1:14
  int<lower=1> Ne[7];                       # Number cases of missings conceptions for each lower limit 1:7, where exposure is also unknown
  int csNc[14];                             # Corresponding cummulative sum of cases
  int csNe[7];                              # Corresponding cummulative sum of cases (including csNc)
   
 ############################################ Used to create mixed array of data/parameters
  int<lower=0> NonMissEx[N];                # Location of non missing data points in Exposure
  int<lower=0> MissCumSumEx[N];             # Cummulative sum of missing data points
  real<lower=0> Exposure[N];                # How long each woman has spent at reproductive age
 
  int<lower=0> NonMissC[N];                 # Location of non missing data points in Conceptions
  int<lower=0> MissCumSumC[N];              # Cummulative sum of missing data points
   
}

parameters {
  vector[2] Theta[3,2];                     # regression parameters for estimation of recruited offspring from conceptions
  vector[2] Imp[3,2];                       # regression parameters for imputation of conceptions from exposure
   
  vector[2] Mu;                             # mean vector of Theta paramters
  vector<lower=0>[2] Sigma;                 #
  corr_matrix[2] Rho;                       # Sigma and Rho create the cov matrix for Theta
 
  vector[2] MuImp;                          #
  vector<lower=0>[2] SigmaImp;              # As above but for imputation model
  corr_matrix[2] RhoImp;                    #
  real<lower=0> ImpSD;
     
  real<lower=1, upper=42> iExposure[NmissEx];  # Paramters for missing exposure data
   
  real<lower=1, upper=15> iCon1[Nc[1]];         # All that follow are parameters for censored conception data.
  real<lower=2, upper=15> iCon2[Nc[2]];         # Since Stan (to my knowlege doesn't allow for mixed constraints in vectors or array)
  real<lower=3, upper=15> iCon3[Nc[3]];         # I code them directly
  real<lower=4, upper=15> iCon4[Nc[4]];
  real<lower=5, upper=15> iCon5[Nc[5]];
  real<lower=6, upper=15> iCon6[Nc[6]];
  real<lower=7, upper=15> iCon7[Nc[7]];
  real<lower=8, upper=15> iCon8[Nc[8]];
  real<lower=9, upper=15> iCon9[Nc[9]];
  real<lower=10, upper=15> iCon10[Nc[10]];
  real<lower=11, upper=15> iCon11[Nc[11]];
  real<lower=12, upper=15> iCon12[Nc[12]];
  real<lower=13, upper=15> iCon13[Nc[13]];
  real<lower=14, upper=15> iCon14[Nc[14]];
 
  real<lower=1, upper=15> iCon1e[Ne[1]];
  real<lower=2, upper=15> iCon2e[Ne[2]];
  real<lower=3, upper=15> iCon3e[Ne[3]];
  real<lower=4, upper=15> iCon4e[Ne[4]];
  real<lower=5, upper=15> iCon5e[Ne[5]];
  real<lower=6, upper=15> iCon6e[Ne[6]];
  real<lower=7, upper=15> iCon7e[Ne[7]];

 
}

transformed parameters{
  real<lower=1,upper=42> impExposure[N];             # Mixed data/parameter array
  real<lower=1,upper=15> impConceptions[N];          # Mixed data/parameter array
  real<lower=1,upper=15> iConceptions[NmissC];       # Mixed constraint parameter array (of conceptions)
 
  cov_matrix[2] Cov;                                 #
  cov_matrix[2] CovImp;                              #
 
######################################### Fill iConceptions
    for(i in 1:csNc[1])
  iConceptions[i]<-iCon1[i];
    for(i in (1+csNc[1]):csNc[2])
  iConceptions[i]<-iCon2[i-csNc[1]];
    for(i in (1+csNc[2]):csNc[3])
  iConceptions[i]<-iCon3[i-csNc[2]];
    for(i in (1+csNc[3]):csNc[4])
  iConceptions[i]<-iCon4[i-csNc[3]];
    for(i in (1+csNc[4]):csNc[5])
  iConceptions[i]<-iCon5[i-csNc[4]];
    for(i in (1+csNc[5]):csNc[6])
  iConceptions[i]<-iCon6[i-csNc[5]];
    for(i in (1+csNc[6]):csNc[7])
  iConceptions[i]<-iCon7[i-csNc[6]];
    for(i in (1+csNc[7]):csNc[8])
  iConceptions[i]<-iCon8[i-csNc[7]];
    for(i in (1+csNc[8]):csNc[9])
  iConceptions[i]<-iCon9[i-csNc[8]];
    for(i in (1+csNc[9]):csNc[10])
  iConceptions[i]<-iCon10[i-csNc[9]];
    for(i in (1+csNc[10]):csNc[11])
  iConceptions[i]<-iCon11[i-csNc[10]];
    for(i in (1+csNc[11]):csNc[12])
  iConceptions[i]<-iCon12[i-csNc[11]];
    for(i in (1+csNc[12]):csNc[13])
  iConceptions[i]<-iCon13[i-csNc[12]];
    for(i in (1+csNc[13]):csNc[14])
  iConceptions[i]<-iCon14[i-csNc[13]];
 
    for(i in (1+csNc[14]):csNe[1])
  iConceptions[i]<-iCon1e[i-csNc[14]];
    for(i in (1+csNe[1]):csNe[2])
  iConceptions[i]<-iCon2e[i-csNe[1]];
    for(i in (1+csNe[2]):csNe[3])
  iConceptions[i]<-iCon3e[i-csNe[2]];
    for(i in (1+csNe[3]):csNe[4])
  iConceptions[i]<-iCon4e[i-csNe[3]];
    for(i in (1+csNe[4]):csNe[5])
  iConceptions[i]<-iCon5e[i-csNe[4]];
    for(i in (1+csNe[5]):csNe[6])
  iConceptions[i]<-iCon6e[i-csNe[5]];
    for(i in (1+csNe[6]):csNe[7])
  iConceptions[i]<-iCon7e[i-csNe[6]];      

############################################ Create mixed data/parameter array
  for(t in 1:N){
   impExposure[t] <- if_else(NonMissEx[t], Exposure[t], iExposure[MissCumSumEx[t]]);
  }
 
  for(t in 1:N){
   impConceptions[t] <- if_else(NonMissC[t],Conceptions[t], iConceptions[MissCumSumC[t]]);
  }
 
########################################### Create Cov matrices
  Cov <- diag_matrix(Sigma) * Rho * diag_matrix(Sigma);
  CovImp <- diag_matrix(SigmaImp) * RhoImp * diag_matrix(SigmaImp);
 
}

model {
real Lambda[N];
#Priors and Parameters
Mu~normal(0,10);
Sigma~gamma(10,.01);
Rho~lkj_corr(2);

MuImp~normal(0,10);
SigmaImp~gamma(10,.01);
RhoImp~lkj_corr(2);

ImpSD~gamma(10,.01);

# "Sample" regression parameters
for(g in 1:3){
for(l in 1:2){
  Theta[g,l] ~ multi_normal(Mu,Cov);
   }}
   
# "Sample" regression parameters  
for(g in 1:3){
for(l in 1:2){
  Imp[g,l] ~ multi_normal(MuImp,CovImp);
   }}
 
# Run regression to impute Conceptions from Exposure time
  for(n in 1:N){
  impConceptions[n] ~ normal((Imp[TimeID[n],LocID[n],1] + Imp[TimeID[n],LocID[n],2]*impExposure[n]),ImpSD)T[1,15];}
 
# Link  
  for(n in 1:N){
   Lambda[n]<-exp( Theta[TimeID[n],LocID[n],1] + Theta[TimeID[n],LocID[n],2]*log(impConceptions[n])) ; }

######################################################################### Main Regressions

# Censored Class 1 - Uncensored  
  for (n in 1:N1) {
  increment_log_prob(poisson_log(Recruited[n],Lambda[n]));
  }
 
# Censored Class 2 - Uncensored Conceptions - Censored Recruitment
# Calculate the difference in CDFs between Y1=min.recruited possible, and Y2=max.recruited.possible

for (n in 1+N1:N2+N1) {
  increment_log_prob(log_diff_exp(poisson_cdf_log(MaxRecruited[n],Lambda[n]), poisson_cdf_log(MinRecruited[n],Lambda[n])));    
  }

##Censored Class 3 - Censored Conceptions - Censored Recruitment
#Calculate the difference in CDFs using inc gamma function for smoothly interpolated poisson_cdf

for (n in 1+N1+N2:N) {
 increment_log_prob(log(  (gamma_q((impConceptions[n]+1.01), Lambda[n])) - (gamma_q((MinRecruited[n]+1), Lambda[n]))    ));
        }

# End Model
}

parts:
Ben,

To fit the model in Stan 1.3 I had to use a while loop to integrate over the cumulative distribution between the minRecruited[n] and floor(impConceptions[n]). The model would run, but it was very slow and inefficient. Effective sample size was small, and the prediction did not do a good job of fitting the data.  I think sampling became a random walk.

 Browsing through the Stan 2.0 manual I noticed that you all had implemented the upper incomplete gamma, so I thought I would give the model a shot with a better coding of the interpolated Poisson CDF.

The model generates good predictions in Stan 2.0 and 2.0.1, when I comment out the offending lines of code, but I would really like to include the censored data for thoroughness.

Also, for diagnostic purposes, the model appears to run OK when I include a negative sign (-) before the log function, but inside the increment_log_prob.

##Censored Class 3 - Censored Conceptions - Censored Recruitment
#Calculate the difference in CDFs using inc gamma function for smoothly interpolated poisson_cdf
for (n in 1+N1+N2:N) {

increment_log_prob(-log(  (gamma_q((impConceptions[n]+1.01), Lambda[n])) - (gamma_q((MinRecruited[n]+1), Lambda[n]))    ));
        }

The predictions for the groups where there are many censored individuals are terrible, but predictiosn in other groups looks great. It is weird that increment_log_prob works to increment the LP_ when the value inside is multiplied by -1, but doesn't work otherwise.

parts:
Given Bob's clue that the bug in gamma_q is limited to extreme cases, I figured I could get the model to run by getting some solid initial values that would put Lambda[n] near its MLE.

The model still would not run, and optimization in command line Stan 2.0.1, spit out some "Non-finite gradient" errors.

So, I started cutting things out of the model. First I got rid of the log prob increments for censoring class 3, still had the error. Then I cut out the log prob increments for censoring class 2, still had the error. Then I cut out the multilevel structure, still had the error. Then I cut out the code for modelling the number of conceptions from time at reproductive age:

# Run regression to impute Conceptions from Exposure time
  for(n in 1:N){
  impConceptions[n] ~ normal((Imp[TimeID[n],LocID[n],1] + Imp[TimeID[n],LocID[n],2]*impExposure[n]),ImpSD)T[1,15];}

And, optimization completed *without* error.

I then went back and ran the model for *only* the above lines of code, and optimization failed, not-surprisingly, with the non-finite gradient error.

So, I cut out the truncation operator, and ran:

# Run regression to impute Conceptions from Exposure time
  for(n in 1:N){

impConceptions[n] ~ normal((Imp[TimeID[n],LocID[n],1] + Imp[TimeID[n],LocID[n],2]*impExposure[n]),ImpSD);}

and optimization completed without error.

This leads me to believe that truncation operator was causing the non-finite gradient error. In my model, I made sure the the truncation limits corresponded to the declared limits of the mixed data/transformed-parameter array. Am I overlooking a flaw in my code, or does the above information suggest that there might be a bug in Stan concerning the Truncation operation    normal(m,s)T[a,b] ?

parts:
Marcus,

I checked out both of your suggestions. My data does not contain zeros, except where the are switched out for parameters. Despite the ugliness of the big blocks of code used for creating these mixed arrays, I have double checked that the resulting transformed parameters are correctly defined. Changing the data declarations didn't solve the problem.

Changing the range of the truncation to T[0,16] also didn't help.

I coded up a simple model:
data {
  int<lower=0> N;                        
  real<lower=1> X[N];  
  real<lower=2,upper=80> Y[N];                            
}

parameters {
 real a;
 real b;      
 real<lower=0> SD;                          
}

model{
a ~ normal(0,10);
b ~ normal(0,10);
SD ~ gamma(10,.01);
for(n in 1:N){
  Y[n] ~ normal((a + b*X[n]),SD)T[2,80];
   }
}    

And made some fake data - attached.
Where the real model for Y is a=0, b=2, and SD=10. Then, values lower than 2 were coerced to =2, and values over 80 were coerced to =80, to created truncated-looking data.

If initial values are set to 0, the BFGS optimization will spit out a few hundred "Error non-finite gradient" warnings, but eventually terminate normally. If inits=1, it will sometimes behave in the same way, and sometimes fail to run. If inits=2 the model never runs.
